title: Reading an American Road Map
description: Unfold a road map and explore directions, symbols, routes, and the scale that puts distances in perspective.
cardDescription: Unfold a road map and explore directions, symbols, routes, and the scale that puts distances in perspective.
focus: This map-reading puzzle uses practical navigation words. A symbol stands for something on the ground, while a scale relates map distance to real distance.
solvingTip: Separate a direction from a map feature. The clue will tell you whether to look for a line, a sign, or a way to measure.
words: Drawing that shows where roads and places are located
Map key that explains the meaning of its symbols
Map feature relating a drawn distance to a real one
Instrument whose needle helps a traveler find north
Chosen course connecting the stops on a trip
Direction opposite south on a road map
Direction opposite north when reading a map
Direction to the right of north on a standard compass rose
Direction opposite east on a compass rose
Line separating two states on a political map
Small supplementary map placed within a larger one
Network of crossing reference lines on a map
US road-distance unit equal to 5280 feet
Bound collection of maps for looking up places

answerNotes.MAP: A map selects information for a purpose. A road map emphasizes routes and settlements rather than showing every object on the ground.
answerNotes.LEGEND: A legend explains symbols. It differs from a compass rose, which shows directions.
answerNotes.SCALE: Scale lets a reader compare map distance with ground distance. It does not show traffic conditions or travel time.
answerNotes.COMPASS: A compass indicates direction. On a map, a compass rose is a drawn guide to directions rather than a moving instrument.
answerNotes.ROUTE: A route is the course followed. A road is a physical feature that can form part of that course.

title: Mountains and Valleys
description: Look across peaks, ridges, slopes, and valleys through clear definitions of the shapes of the land.
cardDescription: Look across peaks, ridges, slopes, and valleys through clear definitions of the shapes of the land.
focus: These landform clues focus on shape and position. A summit is a high point, a ridge extends along a height, and a valley lies between higher ground.
solvingTip: Picture the outline of each feature before trying its name. A crossing letter can distinguish several short landscape words.
words: Highest point reached on a mountain
Long narrow crest of elevated land
Low stretch of land between hills or mountains
Broad elevated area with a relatively level surface
Low crossing route through a mountain range
Pointed top rising above the surrounding mountain slopes
Connected chain or group of mountains
Inclined side of a hill or mountain
Steep exposed face of rock beside higher ground
Deep narrow valley with steep sides
Lower hill near the base of a mountain range
Low land area surrounded by higher terrain
Marked or worn path for walking through mountain country
Natural solid material making up a cliff face

answerNotes.SUMMIT: A summit is a mountain's highest point. A ridge can contain several high points along its length.
answerNotes.RIDGE: A ridge is extended rather than a single peak. Its length helps distinguish it from a summit.
answerNotes.VALLEY: A valley is lower than the land beside it. Valleys may be shaped by flowing water, glaciers, or other processes.
answerNotes.PLATEAU: A plateau has both elevation and a comparatively level top. Flatness alone does not make low land a plateau.
answerNotes.PASS: A mountain pass provides a lower route between higher areas. It is a land feature rather than a ticket in this clue.

title: Following Rivers and Lakes
description: Follow water from a river source toward its mouth, stopping at banks, channels, and lakes along the way.
cardDescription: Follow water from a river source toward its mouth, stopping at banks, channels, and lakes along the way.
focus: The clues distinguish flowing water from a river's source, channel, and banks. Other answers name standing water, shore features, and structures that hold water back.
solvingTip: Notice whether the clue describes the start of a river, its side, its flow, or where it ends.
words: Starting place from which a river flows
Place where a river enters a larger body of water
Deposited landform that can form at a river mouth
Smaller watercourse flowing into a larger river
Land immediately along the side of a river
Inland body of standing water surrounded by land
Small flowing watercourse that may join a river
Movement of water along a river channel
Passage through which a river's water flows
Toward the source rather than the mouth of a river
Land along the edge of a lake
Fast turbulent stretch of a river over an uneven bed
Barrier built to hold back or control flowing water

answerNotes.SOURCE: A source is a river's beginning. It is upstream from its mouth, even when the river flows south to north.
answerNotes.MOUTH: The mouth is the river's outlet. It can open into a lake, another river, or the sea.
answerNotes.DELTA: A delta forms where sediment accumulates near a river's outlet. Not every river mouth has a delta.
answerNotes.TRIBUTARY: A tributary joins another stream or river. The term describes a connection, not a fixed size of channel.
answerNotes.BANK: A river bank borders the channel. In this clue it is neither a financial business nor the entire river valley.

title: Familiar Sights Along the Coast
description: Follow the coast through beaches, bays, sand, boats, and the movement of the sea.
cardDescription: Follow the coast through beaches, bays, sand, boats, and the movement of the sea.
focus: These clues describe ordinary seaside features rather than specialist coastal-science terms.
solvingTip: Try the short weather and water words before the land shapes.
words: Strip of sand or pebbles beside the water
Coastal water inlet partly enclosed by land
Hill of sand shaped by the wind
Sheltered water where boats can stop
Tiny loose grains underfoot at the beach
Ridge of moving water at the coastline
Hard empty covering that may wash onto a beach
Regular rise and fall of coastal water
Land beside the sea, as seen from a boat
Small vessel seen near the coast
Coastal place where ships load and unload
Moving air felt on a seaside walk
Hard natural piece on a stony beach
Seabird often seen over a harbor

answerNotes.COAST: A coast marks the meeting of land and a large body of salt water.
answerNotes.BEACH: Not every beach is sandy; some are covered with stones.
answerNotes.BAY: A bay is a water feature rather than a projecting piece of land.
answerNotes.DUNE: Dunes can form along a coast as well as inland.
answerNotes.HARBOR: A harbor offers protection from more open water.

title: Desert Landscapes of the Southwest
description: Explore dry-country landforms and plants through direct clues about mesas, washes, rocks, and desert growth.
cardDescription: Explore dry-country landforms and plants through direct clues about mesas, washes, rocks, and desert growth.
focus: This Southwest landscape puzzle introduces a few regional words with direct definitions. Desert means very low precipitation, not necessarily constant heat.
solvingTip: Look for a plant, a dry channel, or a landform. Several longer regional terms can be built from shorter crossing answers.
words: Isolated flat-topped hill with steep sides
Isolated steep-sided hill with a comparatively small flat top
Usually dry Southwest channel that carries water after rain
Spiny desert plant with water-storing stems
Water-supported green area within an arid region
Loose grains that may collect in desert dunes
Wind-shaped hill of loose desert grains
Dry streambed that may fill during rain in the Southwest
Plant with swordlike leaves and tall stalks of flowers
Rosette-forming succulent with thick pointed leaves
Aromatic plant name used for several dry-country shrubs
Exposed solid stone visible on a desert slope
Very dry, as a climate with little precipitation
Low scattered woody growth in dry country

answerNotes.MESA: A mesa is a tablelike landform. Its relatively broad top distinguishes it from a smaller butte in common geographic usage.
answerNotes.BUTTE: A butte is typically smaller across the top than a mesa. Both can remain as surrounding rock erodes.
answerNotes.ARROYO: An arroyo is a channel, not a permanent lake. It may be dry much of the time and carry water during runoff.
answerNotes.CACTUS: Many cacti store water in thick stems. Their spines are modified leaves; the term is a plant name rather than a landform.
answerNotes.OASIS: An oasis has a local water supply that supports growth. It does not mean an entire desert receives abundant rain.
